name: Pakistan
card_headline: Pakistan is in open conflict with the Afghan Taliban, fighting militants at home and brokering US-Iran talks, while Field Marshal Munir commands and Imran Khan stays jailed
card_summary: Authorities count more than 2,800 militant attacks and 3,000 deaths since January. [1] Clashes with Afghanistan's Taliban government have run since February, and bilateral trade fell 95 percent. [2] Asim Munir became chief of defence forces under the 27th Amendment. [3] Imran Khan, jailed since 2023, says he may not survive without treatment. [4] Inflation hit 10.3 percent in September and the central bank raised its rate to 12 percent. [5]
card_local: Dawn and The Express Tribune report the 27th Amendment's army powers, Imran Khan's letter on his health, and PICSS data showing 143 militant attacks in October. [3][4][6] Pashto, Balochi and Sindhi-language local sources were not read in this draft.
card_international: AP and Reuters carry Pakistani military claims from the Afghan border and Imran Khan's appeal to the Supreme Court. [1][7] Al Jazeera reports that Pakistan brokered the April US-Iran ceasefire and signed a three-way defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. [8]
card_scholar: Chatham House describes the 27th Amendment as moving Pakistan toward authoritarian rule, and FDD's Long War Journal tracks the border fighting with Afghanistan. [9][10]
context_md: Pakistan has about 240 million people and its Balochistan province, the poorest, holds the Gwadar port and the Reko Diq mine. [11] Imran Khan was removed as prime minister in an April 2022 no-confidence vote, has been in prison since August 2023, and his party was barred from the 2024 election. [12] The Taliban's 2021 return to Kabul hit Pakistan hardest, the International Crisis Group says, because the Afghan Taliban will not act against the Pakistani Taliban (TTP). [13] India put the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance in April 2025 after the Pahalgam attack, which Pakistan denies any role in. [14] The United States designated the Balochistan Liberation Army a foreign terrorist organisation in August 2025. [11] In November 2025 parliament passed the 27th Amendment, which created a chief of defence forces post and a Federal Constitutional Court. [9] The IMF has run a loan programme for Pakistan with reviews through 2026. [15]

sections.title: Militant violence: a September peak, a quieter October and 3,000 dead this year by official count
sections.body_md:
Pakistani authorities say more than 2,800 militant attacks since January have killed 3,000 people, mainly in the northwest and Balochistan, AP reported on 17 October. [1] The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS) counted 143 attacks in October, down 37 percent from 226 in September, with deaths falling from 260 to 111. September had three suicide attacks that killed 45 people and injured 138. [6] The government and PICSS figures come from different sources and are not reconciled in this draft.

The September peak includes an 18 September suicide attack on a police compound that killed 31 people, claimed by Ittehad ul Mujahideen Pakistan, an alliance with TTP roots. [10] On 11 November the TTP claimed an ambush on police vehicles in Kohat district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Authorities reported 10 police and 18 militants dead and alleged the TTP colluded with illegal gold miners. [10] The International Crisis Group counted more than 600 soldiers and police killed by militants in 2025. [13]

Balochistan carries a separate insurgency. The Pakistan Institute for Peace Studies recorded at least 254 attacks there in 2025, about 26 percent more than in 2024, and ACLED reported IED and grenade attacks up more than 65 percent in the first 11 months of 2025. [11] On 24 May a suicide car bomb hit a train carrying soldiers in Quetta and killed at least 24 people. The BLA claimed it. [11] PICSS counted 71 attacks in Balochistan in October against 132 in September. [6]

lenses.local: The Express Tribune carries PICSS's monthly counts, which show attacks falling in October after the September peak. [6]
lenses.international: AP reports the government's totals and the UN mission's count of more than 1,100 civilian casualties from cross-border violence in Afghanistan this year. [1]
lenses.scholar: The International Crisis Group counts more than 600 security personnel killed in 2025, and Yunas Samad of the University of Bradford says suicide tactics are increasingly used by insurgents in the region. [13][11]

sections.title: The Afghan border: "open war" declared in February, air strikes in September, trade down 95 percent
sections.body_md:
On 26 February the Taliban authorities said they had launched offensive operations against Pakistani positions after Pakistani air strikes in Nangarhar and Paktia. The prime minister's spokesperson, Mosharraf Zaidi, said 133 Taliban fighters were killed. An Afghan military source told Al Jazeera that 10 Pakistani soldiers died and 13 outposts were captured. Neither claim was verified. [16] Defence Minister Khwaja Muhammad Asif declared "open war" after the late-February clashes. [2]

On 24 September Pakistan struck 10 locations in Afghanistan from the air, which spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid said hit Kandahar, Paktia and Khost. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar called a drone incursion the day before deliberate and unlawful, and the Taliban denied launching drones. [17] Fighting has recurred since 29 October at Angoor Adda in Paktika and at Torkham, where a clash closed the crossing for five hours on 1 November. [10] The two sides disagree on who fired first. [2]

The economic cost is measurable. Pakistani trade figures show bilateral trade fell 95 percent in fiscal 2026, and an Afghan chamber of commerce official says transit between Pakistan and Central Asia has stopped. [2] The New York Times reported on 24 October that Pakistani officials met anti-Taliban resistance groups, which Pakistan denies. [2] China, Turkiye, Qatar and Saudi Arabia have tried to mediate. [17] Pakistan says TTP leaders have sanctuary in Afghanistan, and Kabul denies it. [1]

lenses.local: Dawn reports the Crisis Group finding that Pakistan is the country worst affected by the Taliban takeover and that Islamabad is likely to strike again if attacks continue. [13]
lenses.international: AP and Al Jazeera report the clashes mainly through Pakistani security officials and spokespeople, with the Taliban often giving no immediate comment. [1][17]
lenses.scholar: FDD's Long War Journal and its podcast argue that Pakistani air strikes have not stopped the TTP, a view from a US security-policy institute. [2][18]

sections.title: The 27th Amendment made Field Marshal Munir chief of defence forces and reshaped the courts
sections.body_md:
The cabinet approved the 27th Amendment on 8 November 2025, the Senate received it on 10 November, the National Assembly passed it on 12 November and President Asif Ali Zardari signed it on 13 November. [9] It created a Chief of Defence Forces post held by the army chief, with authority over the air and naval forces and control of the body that manages the nuclear stockpile. Removal requires a two-thirds parliamentary majority, a five-star officer gets lifetime immunity from prosecution, and the president also gets lifetime immunity. [9]

It also created a Federal Constitutional Court that can override Supreme Court decisions, with the executive and parliament playing a decisive role in appointments. [9] Dawn reported that Asim Munir was named the first chief of defence forces on 4 December 2025 for five years, concurrent with his post as army chief. The amendment abolished the chairman joint chiefs of staff post, and Army Act changes allow his tenure to be reset, which could keep him in office until December 2035. [3]

Amnesty International says the amendment weakened the independence of the higher judiciary and gave broad immunity to military and presidential leaders. [19] A coalition of press freedom groups says the new court coincided with weaker judicial oversight of attacks on journalists. [20] Government statements defending the amendment were not retrieved for this draft.

lenses.local: Dawn calls the CDF appointment the most sweeping restructuring of the military command since the 1970s. [3]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House says the amendment writes the civil-military arrangement in place since 2018 into the constitution. [9]

sections.title: Imran Khan: a health dispute and a court order his side says was not carried out
sections.body_md:
Khan was removed as prime minister in April 2022 and has been jailed since 5 August 2023. Al Jazeera's August summary says he serves 14 years for corruption, his wife Bushra Bibi seven, and that the couple received a further 17 years in December 2025 in a state-gifts case. [12] Reuters reports on 16 November that all his convictions except one have been suspended or overturned and that appeals are pending. [7] This draft could not reconcile the two accounts of his legal status.

In a 16 November letter to the chief justices, Khan wrote that doctors warned he is highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest, that his blood pressure reached 192 and 193 on 10 November, and that his right eye lost 85 percent of its vision. [4] A three-member Supreme Court bench ordered on 18 August that he be moved to Shifa International Hospital and allowed weekly family meetings. Khan says the order was not implemented. He was taken to the state hospital PIMS instead, and a medical board later reported improved right-eye vision and did not recommend a transfer. [4]

Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry rejected the allegations, said Khan's health is satisfactory and that he has been taken to PIMS eight times. [4] Amnesty International said in August that Khan had not seen family for over eight months. UN Special Rapporteur Alice Jill Edwards said solitary confinement of up to 23 hours a day could amount to torture. Minister of State Tallal Chaudhry said his conditions are under judicial oversight. [12]

lenses.local: The Express Tribune prints Khan's letter and the government's rebuttal side by side. [4]
lenses.international: Reuters and Al Jazeera report both the appeal and the government's position, and Al Jazeera adds Amnesty and the UN rapporteur. [7][12]

sections.title: Inflation is back above 10 percent as the IMF clears another $1.2 billion
sections.body_md:
IMF staff reached agreement on 8 October on the fourth review of the Extended Fund Facility, which would release about $1.2 billion after board approval: roughly $1.0 billion under the EFF and $210 million under the climate-focused Resilience and Sustainability Facility. Total disbursements would reach about $5.7 billion. [21] In May the board released about $1.32 billion, bringing the total to about $4.8 billion. [22][15] The staff conditions include phasing out the fuel support scheme, keeping monetary policy tight, adjusting electricity tariffs and advancing privatization. [21]

Consumer inflation was 10.3 percent in September, with core inflation at about 8.4 percent against a target range of 5 to 7 percent. The State Bank raised its policy rate by 50 basis points to 12 percent on a 9-1 vote, citing the Middle East conflict, energy prices and wheat supply disruptions. [5] In May the IMF had projected average inflation of 7.2 percent for fiscal 2026. [15]

The World Bank's regional report says Pakistan holds about 48 percent of the people living below $3 a day in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region, and that its poverty rate rose 6.4 percentage points at that line between 2018-19 and 2024-25. [23] For investors the minerals sector is the main opening: the United States announced $1.25 billion for critical-minerals mining at Reko Diq in December 2025, where Barrick Gold operates. [11]

lenses.local: Geo News, ProPakistani and The Express Tribune report the IMF terms, the 12 percent rate and the poverty figures. [22][21][5]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera ties the Reko Diq investment and China's roughly $65 billion corridor to the Balochistan security problem. [11]
lenses.scholar: The IMF and the World Bank are the main sources, and both describe reserves rebuilding while poverty rises. [15][23]

sections.title: Mediator in Tehran, treaty partner of Riyadh, and a water ruling India rejects
sections.body_md:
The United States and Israel began striking Iran on 28 February. Pakistan brokered a ceasefire on 8 April and hosted the highest-level direct US-Iran talks since 1979. A 14-point memorandum, the Islamabad MoU, followed in June, but its 60-day window expired in mid-August without an extension. Munir made his fifth trip to Tehran since April on 20 October. [8] Qatar does much of the detailed negotiating while Pakistan provides political access to both sides. [8]

Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on 7 August, under which an attack on one is treated as an attack on all three. [8][24] Pakistan says the pact is aimed at no country, and President Trump welcomed it. [24] Analysts told Al Jazeera that the Saudi commitments weaken Pakistan's standing as a neutral mediator, and Pakistan's Foreign Office says its forces in Saudi Arabia will not cross into Yemen. [8]

On water, the Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled unanimously that India cannot unilaterally suspend the Indus Waters Treaty, which it said remains fully in force. India did not take part and calls the court illegally constituted. The ruling has no enforcement mechanism, and the Permanent Indus Commission has not met since May 2022. [14] Chatham House notes that perennial snow and ice cover in the basin fell by up to 24.8 percent between 2001 and 2021. [25]

lenses.international: Al Jazeera reports the mediation, the defence pact and the Hague ruling, and relies on named Pakistani officials and outside analysts. [8][14]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House argues that restoring data sharing and dispute resolution under the treaty would help rebuild trust. [25]

sections.title: Press, Baloch activists and Afghan refugees: where rights groups press hardest
sections.body_md:
On 25 February the Committee to Protect Journalists and 17 other organisations wrote to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif about a sustained deterioration of media freedom. They asked for the release of Sohrab Barkat, held under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), repeal or substantial amendment of PECA, and an end to deportations of at-risk Afghan journalists. [20]

Amnesty's 2026 annual report, as relayed by Dawn, says authorities used cybercrime and anti-terror laws against dissent and selectively pulled advertising from critical newspapers. It records three Baloch protesters killed by law enforcement on 21 March and more than 100 PTI leaders and activists convicted over the 9 May 2023 protests. [19] Amnesty also says the Baloch Students Organization head Jiand Baloch was taken from his home on 24 July, the third time he has been forcibly disappeared. [26]

Human Rights Watch reported on 21 April that Pakistan had deported more than 146,000 Afghans in 2026, detained people holding valid visas, and forcibly returned at least nine Afghan journalists since January, according to Reporters Without Borders. [27] No Pakistani government response to these findings was retrieved for this draft.

lenses.local: Dawn carries the CPJ coalition letter and Amnesty's annual findings. [20][19]
lenses.international: Human Rights Watch interviewed eight Afghans in Pakistan and four who had returned to Afghanistan. [27]

sections.title: The 2026 monsoon: 107 dead by late July, after 1,037 in 2025
sections.body_md:
Rain-related flooding had killed at least 107 people and injured 344 since late June, the National Disaster Management Authority said on 27 July. More than half the deaths came from house or roof collapses. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had the most deaths (55), followed by Punjab (36). [28] An irrigation official in Punjab described the situation as very alarming, with about 400 square kilometres under water across the Lahore and Gujranwala divisions, and Lahore opened at least 17 relief camps. [28]

Heavy flooding in 2025 killed 1,037 people and displaced two million. [28] The monsoon was expected to continue to September, and this draft did not retrieve a final 2026 toll. [28]

Flood preparedness is also part of the IMF programme. The Resilience and Sustainability Facility targets disaster resilience, water pricing, and federal-provincial disaster coordination, and the October staff agreement would release about $210 million under it. [15][21]

lenses.international: Al Jazeera quotes NDMA figures and a Punjab irrigation official on the July flooding. [28]
lenses.scholar: The IMF treats climate and disaster resilience as a programme priority. [15]

scores.coverage_basis: AP and Reuters file on Pakistan regularly, with peaks around the Iran mediation, Afghan border clashes and Imran Khan's health. [1][7] Dawn and The Express Tribune produce daily English-language coverage, and FDD, Chatham House and the Crisis Group publish on the border and the army. [3][10][9] Reporting on Balochistan and on Afghan deportations is thinner and depends on rights groups. [11][27]

severity.basis: Authorities count about 3,000 deaths from more than 2,800 attacks since January, and Pakistan and Afghan Taliban forces have exchanged fire and air strikes since February. [1][17]
Monsoon floods killed at least 107 people by late July after 1,037 in 2025, and Pakistan deported more than 146,000 Afghans by April. [28][27]
The 27th Amendment put the army chief and president beyond prosecution, Khan is in solitary confinement, and press groups report a sustained decline in media freedom. [9][12][20]
Inflation was 10.3 percent in September, the policy rate is 12 percent, and the poverty rate at $3 a day rose 6.4 points since 2018-19, though the IMF programme continues. [5][23][21]
Border fighting with Afghanistan widened in September and October, the rate was raised in October, and the PICSS count fell in October after a September peak. [17][5][6]

parts.basis: The United States, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye deal with Pakistan on defence and minerals, and China's roughly $65 billion corridor runs through Balochistan. [24][11]
Pakistan is a regional economy of about 240 million people with a minerals opening at Reko Diq, but its weight in world trade is limited. [11]
Fighting with Afghanistan has halted bilateral trade, the Indus dispute involves another nuclear-armed neighbour, and Pakistan is a party to the Iran talks. [2][14][8]
Pakistan hosts Afghan refugees it is now deporting, and over 5.4 million Afghans had been pushed out of Iran and Pakistan since October 2023. [27]

The Hague ruling on the Indus treaty is the first international court ruling on whether India's suspension is valid, and Pakistan's army chief now controls the nuclear stockpile's managing body. [14][9]

summary: Pakistan matters beyond its borders through its nuclear arsenal, its role as US-Iran go-between, its Saudi and Turkish defence ties, and its fight with the Afghan Taliban government. [9][8][24][10]
Trade and finance matter less: its economy is mid-sized and depends on IMF disbursements. [21]
gi.up: A direct India-Pakistan military exchange, a collapse of the Iran ceasefire that draws in Pakistan's Saudi commitments, or an Afghan border war that escalates to Kabul and Peshawar.
gi.down: A durable Pakistan-Afghanistan truce, restored Indus treaty data sharing and a settled Iran deal.

gaps: Local sourcing is English-language only: Dawn, The Express Tribune, Geo and ProPakistani were read; Urdu, Pashto, Balochi and Sindhi outlets were not.
No Baloch, Pashtun or Afghan outlet was read, so the Balochistan and Afghan border accounts rest on Pakistani officials, AP, Al Jazeera and rights groups.
Casualty claims in the February and September Afghan clashes come from the two governments and are unverified.
Imran Khan's legal status differs between Al Jazeera (14 plus 17 years) and Reuters (all but one conviction suspended or overturned).
The ICG, World Bank and PICSS findings were read through news reports, not the original documents.
The Mecca pact article and the Hague ruling dates are inferred (August 2026 and Monday 31 August).
The government's defence of the 27th Amendment and its response to the HRW and Amnesty findings were not retrieved.
The final 2026 monsoon toll and any government figure on Afghan returns after April were not retrieved.
No documentary or photo essay was verified, so the media list is empty.
Scholar coverage leans on think-tank commentary; few peer-reviewed sources were reviewed.
